transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Priya Shah (AE, Redwood), Marco Li (SE, Redwood), Elena Martinez (CTO, NovusHealth), Marcus Reed (Lead Engineer), Jae Kim (SRE), Sophie Laurent (Product)

Summary (auto):
Quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation streaming, parameter choices (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and resilient retry/backoff patterns for production. Customer cares about latency targets (p95 < 250ms for short replies), data residency in EU, SOC2 controls, and graceful degradation to smaller/faster models when capacity spikes. Discussed Console Optimize suggestions for batching and cache profiles.

Transcript:
[00:00] Priya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Priya from Redwood, i'll hand over to Marco for the dev walkthrough in a minute. brief intro — we want to show hosted chat streaming, how to tune params, and common retry patterns.
[00:12] Elena: thanks, our CTO is on this call to understand feasibility — Marcus is our eng lead and Jae is SRE. main goals: low-latency UIs for clinicians, predictable cost, and no PHI leaving EU.
[00:28] Marco: great — quick agenda: 1) live demo of streaming chat via the API, 2) params and quality/latency tradeoffs, 3) retry and backoff patterns, 4) console tips and Optimize recommendations. we'll also cover VPC/private concerns briefly.
[00:40] Marcus: awesome, and if possible show how to do idempotency and detect partial stream failures.
[00:46] Marco: absolutely — we'll show a small node/python snippet and a retry wrapper we recommend.
[01:05] Marco: ok sharing screen — here's a simple streaming example, we open a websocket-like stream, server sends partial deltas as tokens come out. note the initial token latency is usually the important metric for UX.
[01:22] Marco: in this example we set temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 150 — lower temperature makes replies more deterministic for clinical guidance.
[01:37] Jae: question: for short replies ~30 tokens, can we hit p95 < 250ms?
[01:43] Marco: depends on model and region — for our verified small-gen model in eu-west we typically see 80–180ms cold p50 and p95 around 200–300ms for short sequences. for stricter SLOs we recommend dedicated or smaller quantized variants.
[01:58] Priya: just to call out, we also have config routing policies — you can route by latency tier so critical traffic goes to dedicated pools and background tasks to cheaper variants.
[02:12] Elena: are there built-in fallbacks? we need graceful degradation when the primary model is saturated.
[02:18] Marco: yes — you can specify model variants in the request policy or use a console rollout. typical pattern is primary -> lower-cost quantized variant -> cached canned responses. Console has canary/automatic fallback rules.
[02:33] Marcus: hmm, what about token counting and cost estimates? we have lots of short messages, would batching help?
[02:41] Marco: batching helps throughput but can add latency. for interactive short messages, we usually rely on prefix/KV cache and request-level caching for repeated prompts. Optimize can analyze traffic and suggest batch sizes and cache TTLs to reduce per-token cost.
[03:02] Sophie: can you show retry logic? we had a previous vendor where retries caused duplicate ops in our backend.
[03:10] Marco: good point — avoid blind retries that re-run side effects. for idempotency we recommend request ids and server-side dedupe. also, for streaming specifically, use resume tokens or check for incomplete streams; our SDK includes a small helper to detect partial stream termination and re-request only missing segments.
[03:30] Marco: demo snippet: client sends X-Request-Id, if stream ends unexpectedly we do an exponential backoff with jitter: 200ms -> 600ms -> 1.8s capped at 8s, and flag to the user "trying to recover". if repeated failures, fallback to a fast local policy.
[03:55] Marcus: are retry counts configurable per route?
[03:58] Priya: yes — route-level policies in Console allow you to set max retries, backoff base, and fallback model.
[04:10] Elena: what about encryption of logs and KV cache? PHI is sensitive.
[04:15] Marco: all persisted logs and cache entries can be configured to use customer KMS (bring-your-own-keys) in Private deployments. For Hosted we have encryption at rest and in transit, and we support contractual terms for EU data residency. we'll send the security pack.
[04:31] Jae: audit logs? we need graded RBAC and SSO.
[04:35] Priya: Redwood Console supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit trails per token. We'll include screenshots in the security packet.
[04:45] Marcus: latency vs cost tradeoffs — if we move to quantized models do we lose quality?
[04:50] Marco: slight drops in rare cases, Optimize provides A/B eval harnesses to compare model variants on your prompt set and quantify regressions. often quantized 4-bit models perform near full-fp for shorter responses.
[05:08] Sophie: can console show per-route token spend so product can monitor cost per feature?
[05:12] Priya: yes, Console has per-route and per-model token breakdowns, plus token-level cost attributions and anomaly alerts.
[05:21] Marco: back to streaming params — temperature/top_p examples: for deterministic outputs (legal/clinical) we suggest temp 0–0.3 and top_p 0.7–0.95. for creative assistant flows increase temperature. max_tokens should be capped to avoid runaway costs.
[05:40] Marcus: any guardrails for hallucination?
[05:43] Marco: combine system prompts with grounding sources, use reranking/QA-check prompts, and run lightweight safety evals pre-commit. Optimize can surface regressions from a reference eval set.
[05:58] Elena: we want to run a short pilot — what would you need?
[06:02] Priya: supply a representative prompt set, acceptance criteria (latency, accuracy measures), and preferred PW/SLA targets. we'll set up a trial account with a sandbox model and include sample scripts.
[06:15] Marcus: how long to spin up sandbox?
[06:17] Priya: sandbox is immediate for hosted API — we can give you credentials today and a 2-week pilot window by default. dedicated/Private takes more lead time.
[06:28] Jae: can we test on eu-only infra?
[06:31] Marco: yes hosted eu regions are available; if you need strict residency we can discuss Private with customer-managed network.
[06:38] Marco: switching to console — here's the Optimize tab; it suggests batching 4->8 for your traffic pattern but flagged that you have many 1–2 token prompts so it suggests prefix caching instead.
[06:55] Sophie: what's prefix caching?
[06:57] Marco: caching the common initial context or static system prompt so the runtime can reuse KV cache and avoid recomputing early layers. big wins for short interactive messages.
[07:12] Marcus: any gotchas for streaming when using caching?
[07:16] Marco: you need to ensure the cache key includes the right prompt context; if clients send variable user metadata you could miss cache hits. also be careful with personalization and PHI — don't cache sensitive content unless it's encrypted per KMS policy.
[07:32] Elena: ok good. can you email the example code and the security docs?
[07:36] Priya: yes — we'll send the security pack and a small repo with node/python streaming examples and the retry helper.
[07:44] Marcus: about fallbacks — if primary is overloaded we prefer graceful fallback to a smaller model not an error to the user. how does Redwood handle that?
[07:52] Marco: server-side policy can automatically route to fallback variants. you can set a latency threshold; if p95 crosses it, traffic is shifted. there's also a circuit-breaker so if the fallback fails you can return a canned response or cached summary.
[08:07] Sophie: will that require code changes?
[08:10] Marco: minimal — mostly route config in Console; clients should handle the small differences in output shape when switching variants.
[08:20] Elena: what KPIs do you recommend we track during pilot?
[08:23] Priya: latency p50/p95, token cost per feature, quality delta vs baseline (we can help instrument), error rate and partial stream incidents, and user-visible fallback rate.
[08:37] Marcus: can you demo partial stream detection quickly?
[08:40] Marco: yes — here's a synthetic stream where the server drops mid-output; our SDK emits an "incomplete_stream" event and the retry helper resumes from the last confirmed token id. We'll include this helper in the repo.
[09:02] Jae: any rate-limits we should be aware of?
[09:05] Marco: by default hosted has soft rate limits per account; they can be raised for pilots. Console shows quota and current usage.
[09:14] Elena: legal/procurement — we'll need contract language around data processing and breach handling.
[09:18] Priya: we'll include standard DPA language and can escalate to legal for custom terms.
[09:24] Sophie: timeline: if we start pilot early April, can we have a quick sync in mid April?
[09:28] Priya: yes let's target week of 2026-04-13 for a pilot review.
[09:33] Marco: wrapping up — I'll push the code examples to a shared repo and email links.
[09:40] Priya: thanks all. quick recap of next steps: security pack, code samples, send pilot agreement + pricing, customer to provide prompt set and SLOs, schedule pilot kickoff.
[09:53] Elena: thanks, appreciate the clear patterns — feel more confident about hosted approach if we can lock data residency and test fallback behavior.
[10:05] Priya: perfect. we'll follow up after the call with materials and a proposed pilot timeline.
[10:12] Meeting ends.
